questions.question: What is component scanning in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Spring Boot component scanning explained
questions.direct_answer: Component scanning is the mechanism Spring uses to automatically find and register beans. When the application starts, Spring scans packages for classes annotated with @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, @RestController (and other meta-annotations). It registers them as beans in the ApplicationContext, enabling dependency injection.
questions.interviewer_intent: Component scanning is fundamental to how Spring works — test whether the candidate understands automatic bean registration.

sections.content: Component scanning is how Spring finds your classes without you having to list them all manually. When Spring Boot starts, it scans your package — the one containing the main class — and all sub-packages. Any class it finds with @Component on it, or an annotation that's meta-annotated with @Component like @Service, @Repository, @Controller, gets picked up and registered as a bean. That bean is then available for @Autowired injection. Without component scanning, you'd have to define every bean manually in a @Configuration class — the approach that was used before annotation-based configuration existed.
@SpringBootApplication includes @ComponentScan which scans the main class's package and all sub-packages.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller?
questions.title: @Component vs @Service vs @Repository vs @Controller
questions.direct_answer: All four register a class as a Spring bean — @Service, @Repository, and @Controller are all meta-annotated with @Component. The difference is semantic and functional: @Repository enables Spring's exception translation (SQL exceptions to DataAccessException). @Controller integrates with Spring MVC. @Service has no extra behavior — it's a documentation annotation for the service layer.
questions.interviewer_intent: Very common question — candidates often know they're all beans but miss the @Repository exception translation difference.

sections.content: From a bean registration standpoint, they're all the same — all four are detected by component scan and registered as beans. The differences are layered on top. @Repository gets one functional benefit: Spring wraps your data access methods with a PersistenceExceptionTranslationProxy that converts JDBC SQLExceptions and Hibernate exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy. This means your service layer only needs to catch Spring exceptions, not database-specific ones. @Controller tells Spring MVC this class handles HTTP requests and enables method-level request mapping. @Service is purely a semantic marker — it has no extra behavior. Use the right annotation for the right layer regardless.

questions.question: What is the default component scan base package in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Default component scan package in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot scans the package containing the @SpringBootApplication class and all sub-packages by default. If your main class is in com.example.myapp, Spring scans com.example.myapp, com.example.myapp.service, com.example.myapp.repository, etc. Classes in com.example.other (a sibling package) are NOT scanned.
questions.interviewer_intent: The default scan base is a frequent source of 'bean not found' bugs — tests practical understanding.

sections.content: This is why the placement of your main application class matters. The convention is to put the main class in the root package — not inside a sub-package, not at the class's package root but in the topmost package of your application. If you put the main class in com.example.myapp, everything in that package and below gets scanned. If a class is in com.example.config, which is at the same level as myapp rather than inside it, it won't be found. This causes 'No qualifying bean of type' errors that confuse people until they check package names. The fix is either move the class or explicitly configure the scan packages.
Main class placement = scan root. Put it in your top-level application package, not in a sub-package.

questions.question: How do you configure component scanning to include additional packages?
questions.title: Configuring @ComponentScan base packages
questions.direct_answer: Use @ComponentScan(basePackages = {"com.example.myapp", "com.other.util"}) to specify additional packages. Or use basePackageClasses to specify type-safe marker classes whose packages are then scanned. This is needed when some components live outside the default scan path.
questions.interviewer_intent: Practical configuration knowledge — shows the candidate can work in non-trivial project structures.

sections.content: If you need to scan additional packages — say a shared utilities library in a different package — you can override the default scan. Add @ComponentScan directly to your @SpringBootApplication class with a basePackages list. Note: once you specify basePackages, the default package (the main class's package) is no longer included automatically — you must add it explicitly in the list. An alternative that avoids magic strings is basePackageClasses — you reference an actual class in each package you want scanned, and Spring derives the package from it. Refactoring-safe.
Specifying basePackages replaces the default. Include your own package plus any additions.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Component and @Bean?
questions.title: @Component vs @Bean in Spring
questions.direct_answer: @Component is a class-level annotation — Spring detects and registers the class via component scan. @Bean is a method-level annotation in a @Configuration class — you write a factory method that creates and returns the bean. @Bean gives you more control over instantiation. Use @Component for your own classes; @Bean for third-party classes you can't annotate.
questions.interviewer_intent: Common interview question that tests understanding of Spring's two bean registration mechanisms.

sections.content: The key difference is who controls instantiation. With @Component, Spring instantiates the class using reflection — you don't control the constructor call. With @Bean, you write the factory method and you control exactly how the object is created. The practical implication: @Component only works on classes you own and can annotate. If you're using a third-party library class — say a RestTemplate or an ObjectMapper from Jackson — you can't add @Component to it. Instead you write a @Configuration class with a @Bean method that creates and configures the instance your way.

questions.question: What is bean scope in Spring and what are the common scopes?
questions.title: Spring bean scopes — singleton vs prototype
questions.direct_answer: Bean scope controls how many instances Spring creates. Singleton (default): one instance per ApplicationContext, shared across all injections. Prototype: a new instance each time the bean is requested. Web scopes: request (one per HTTP request), session (one per HTTP session). Most service and repository beans are singleton.
questions.interviewer_intent: Bean scope is frequently asked — test whether the candidate understands the singleton default and its implications.

sections.content: The default scope is singleton — Spring creates one instance of your bean and every @Autowired injection gets that same instance. This is why your @Service beans must be stateless — if you store request-specific data in a field, concurrent requests will corrupt each other's data since they share the same object. Prototype scope creates a fresh instance every time someone requests the bean. It's less common because it bypasses normal injection — Spring injects the prototype bean once, not on every method call, so you often need ApplicationContext.getBean() to really get a fresh instance each time.
Singleton = shared instance — must be stateless. Prototype = new instance per injection. Singleton is the default.

questions.question: What is @Autowired and how does Spring resolve which bean to inject?
questions.title: @Autowired and Spring dependency injection
questions.direct_answer: @Autowired instructs Spring to inject a dependency. Spring resolves it by type first — it looks for a bean whose type matches. If there are multiple candidates of the same type, it resolves by name (matching the field name). Use @Qualifier("beanName") to be explicit when there's ambiguity. Constructor injection is preferred over field injection.
questions.interviewer_intent: @Autowired is used everywhere — test understanding of the resolution mechanism and best practices.

sections.content: @Autowired tells Spring 'inject a bean here.' Spring looks at the type of the field or parameter — if there's exactly one bean of that type, it injects it. If there are multiple implementations — say two classes implementing the same interface — Spring gets confused and throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. To fix that, add @Qualifier with the specific bean name, or annotate one implementation with @Primary. The modern best practice is constructor injection over field injection. Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit, enables final fields, and makes the class testable without a Spring context.
Prefer constructor injection — final fields, no Spring dependency in tests, explicit contract. Spring 4.3+ injects single-constructor beans without @Autowired.
